planting.note: Plant dormant tubers about 3 inches deep in gritty, sharply drained soil in late summer or fall, just ahead of its unusual autumn bloom.

directions: Arum pictum is a Mediterranean aroid from Corsica, Sardinia, and the Balearic Islands with an unusual reversed schedule: deep blackish-purple, carrion-scented spathes emerge directly from bare ground in autumn, followed only afterward by glossy, plain dark-green arrow-shaped leaves that persist through winter before going dormant by late spring. Plant dormant tubers in late summer or fall about 3 inches deep in gritty, sharply drained soil in part sun to light shade, and withhold water completely during its summer dormancy to prevent rot. It is less hardy than the related Arum italicum and performs best where summers are hot and dry, or where tubers can be grown in pots and sheltered from prolonged winter wet in colder zones. Divide offset tubers after foliage dies back to propagate.

planting.note: Plant dormant tubers about 3 inches deep in gritty, fast-draining soil in fall so foliage can establish over winter ahead of spring flowers.

directions: Arum creticum, native to Crete and parts of southwestern Turkey, is the most garden-friendly oddity among Mediterranean arums: its golden-yellow spathes, carried on slender stalks above the foliage in spring, release a genuinely pleasant sweet fragrance rather than the carrion smell typical of the genus. Plant dormant tubers in fall about 3 inches deep in gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun to light shade; arrow-shaped leaves emerge in fall or winter, flowers follow in spring, and the whole plant dies back by early summer as the tuber goes dormant. Keep it dry during summer dormancy to avoid rot, and site it where its late-spring disappearing act is masked by later-emerging companions. Offset tubers can be lifted and divided once foliage has withered.

planting.note: Plant dormant tubers 3 to 4 inches deep in gritty, sharply drained soil in fall; it needs a hot, dry summer rest to perform reliably.

directions: Arum dioscoridis is a dramatic eastern Mediterranean species from Turkey, Cyprus, and the Levant, bearing a broad, pale cream to greenish spathe heavily blotched and streaked with deep maroon-purple that surrounds a nearly black spadix; the strong dung-like scent is a reliable fly magnet in spring. Plant dormant tubers in fall roughly 3 to 4 inches deep in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun to part shade, letting the arrow-shaped leaves emerge over winter ahead of the spring flowers before the whole plant goes summer-dormant. It is more cold-tender than Arum italicum and needs a hot, dry summer rest, making it best suited to raised beds, rock gardens, or pots in climates with wet summers. Propagate by dividing the offset tubers produced around the mother tuber.

planting.note: Plant tubers 2 to 3 inches deep in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in part to full shade; confine it, as it spreads readily by bulbils.

directions: Pinellia pedatisecta is a Chinese woodland aroid distinguished from its smaller relatives by leaves divided into five to eleven narrow, finger-like lobes arranged in a fan, giving the foliage a striking bird's-foot or dragon's-claw outline. In summer it produces slender green spathes whose spadix appendix extends into a long, thread-like tail that can trail well beyond the spathe itself. Plant tubers in spring about 2 to 3 inches deep in moist, humus-rich soil in part to full shade, and expect it to multiply steadily by aerial bulbils, so give it a contained bed or be ready to share the extras. It dies back to its tuber each winter and returns reliably in spring; divide offset tubers or collect self-sown bulbils to propagate.

planting.note: Plant small dormant tubers about 2 inches deep in late summer in extremely sharp-draining, gritty soil; it resents any summer moisture.

directions: Biarum tenuifolium is a diminutive Mediterranean aroid, found from Italy through the Balkans to Turkey, grown by collectors for its oddity value: the narrow, twisted, dark maroon-to-blackish spathe emerges with almost no stalk directly at soil level in late summer, well before any leaves appear, and gives off a distinctly carrion-like scent to lure pollinating flies. Plant the small dormant tubers in late summer about 2 inches deep in extremely sharp-draining, gritty soil in part sun, where the strap-shaped leaves follow in autumn and persist through winter before the plant retreats underground for a dry summer dormancy. It is best grown in a raised bed, trough, or pot where its drainage and dry-summer needs can be controlled. Propagate by separating the small offset tubers that form around the parent tuber.
